meta.title: Bridge Tutor
meta.course: Derrick Browne Beginners' Bridge / Will Jenner-O'Shea resources

chapters.title: Basics
chapters.summary: How a hand is played: longest suit, following suit, trumps, and the shape of a simple auction.
concepts: Open your longest suit when you have a reasonable hand.
Partner raising shows support for your suit.
Follow suit if you can; if not, you may trump or discard.
A good plan in a trump contract: draw trumps, then cash side-suit winners.

chapters.title: Early Bidding
chapters.summary: The core of the modern 5-card major system: when to open, and how to raise.
concepts: Open with 12+ high-card points (HCP).
To open 1♥ or 1♠ you need 5+ cards in that major.
A 1♣ or 1♦ open can be as short as 3 cards (when you lack a 5-card major).
Partner needs only 6+ points to respond.
A simple raise (e.g. 1♠–2♠) shows 3+ support and about 6–10 points.

chapters.title: Game Plan
chapters.summary: When the partnership has enough strength, bid game (3NT, 4♥, 4♠, or 5 of a minor).
concepts: Game needs roughly 25+ combined points (majors/NT) or a bit more in minors.
With a known fit and enough points, bid the game yourself — do not stop in part-score.
Prefer major-suit or no-trump games to minor-suit games when both are possible.
Count winners and losers before you play the first card.

chapters.title: Responder Shifts
chapters.summary: When you cannot raise partner's suit, bid a new suit (a shift) to search for a better fit.
concepts: A new suit by responder is forcing for one round (partner must bid again).
Show a 4+ card major at the one-level when you can.
Opener's rebid clarifies strength and shape.
Keep searching until you find an 8-card fit or settle in no-trumps.

chapters.title: Opening 1NT
chapters.summary: A balanced hand with 15–17 HCP opens 1NT — the backbone of the strong no-trump system.
concepts: 1NT = 15–17 HCP, balanced (no singleton/void; usually no 5-card major in this course).
Partner can raise to 3NT with enough combined points (~25+).
With a long major and game values, partner may offer a choice of games.
In no-trumps, establish your longest suit early.

chapters.title: Overcalls and Doubles
chapters.summary: When the opponents open, you can still enter: overcall a good suit, or double for takeout.
concepts: An overcall shows a good 5+ card suit and roughly 10+ points.
A takeout double shows opening values and support for the unbid suits.
After partner doubles, you must respond — bid your longest suit (or NT with a stopper).
Competitive auctions still aim for the right strain and level.

auction.annotation: You are dealer, and Spades is your longest suit, so you bid 1S
auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You are the Dealer, so you get to bid first. You have a reasonably good hand, and your longest suit is Spades, so you open the bidding with 1S.

auction.annotation: Partner also likes Spades, so bids to 2S
auction.teaching: Your partner also likes Spades, so raises the Spades.

auction.annotation: No reason to go any higher (yet!)
auction.teaching: There are reasons go bid higher than just 2S, but not yet!

play.teaching: They lead the Jack of Hearts against your 2S contract.
Your Queen probably won't win, so you might as well not play it.
They lead another Heart,
and you can try your Queen,
which loses to the Ace.
If the Defenders try leading a third Heart,
you have no Hearts, so can play any card, including a TRUMP. Any trump beats anything else.
A good plan when you are playing in a trump suit is to lead out some Spades,
winning,
and again.
The opponents have run out of Spades, but you have some left.
Now lead your other cards,
winning some extra tricks.

auction.annotation: You have a good hand and Hearts is your longest suit
auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You are the Dealer, so you get to bid first. You have a good hand and Hearts is your longest suit, so yuo open 1H.

auction.annotation: No reason to go any higher (yet!)

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 2H contract.
You can win the lead,
and lead some trumps,
trying to win.
Lead another Heart,
and win that one as well.
The opponents have no Hearts left, so you can play Spade winners.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You are the Dealer, so you get to bid first. You have a good hand and Hearts is your longest suit, so yuo open 1H.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You have a good hand, and you are the Dealer, so you open the bidding. Always open with your LOGNEST suit first.
Your partner doesn't like Diamonds, so offers Hearts.
You don't like Hearts, so you now offer 1S. Since Spades are the highest ranked suit, you can bid 1S over 1H.
Partner show that they also like Spades, and you have found your trump suit.

play.teaching: They lead the Four of Clubs against your 2S contract.
They win the first trick.
They lead a Club back,
and win that as well.
They try a third Club,
and you trump.
You should try to draw the trumps,
and count them as you go.
Draw enough trumps that the opponents run out.
Then play other suits. In Hearts you should play a Heart,
and another Heart,
even though the Ace is missing. After losing the Ace, the rest of your Hearts are winners.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You have a good hand, and you are the Dealer, so you open the bidding. Always open with your LOGNEST suit first.

auction.annotation: You have a good hand, with long Spades
auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You open 1S, with a good hand and long Spades.
Your partner confirms that Spades will be a good trump suit.

play.teaching: They lead the Queen of Hearts against your 2S contract.
You can win the lead,
and try to draw some of the opponent's trumps.
After the opponents are out of trumps, play other suits.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. You open 1S, with a good hand and long Spades.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. East Passes as the Dealer, since they don't have 12+ points.
You open 1S, showing 12+ points, and to open a Major (Hearts or Spades) 5+ cards in that suit.
Your partner raises to 2S, showing 3 or more Spades, so you know that you have a Spade fit. Partner only needs 6+ points to Respond.
There are reasons to bid higher, but not yet.

play.teaching: They lead the Jack of Diamonds against your 2S contract.
You can win the lead right away,
and should try to draw the opponent's trumps.
They have the Ace,
and later the King, which they will win,
but you can mop up all of their little trumps.
You can then win several tricks from the other suits, Hearts,
and Diamonds,
and lose a couple of Clubs along the way.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. East Passes as the Dealer, since they don't have 12+ points.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. West passes, since they don't have 12+ points.
Your partner opens 1C, showing 12+ points and maybe only 3+ Clubs.
You Respond 1S, showing 6+ points and 4+ Spades.
Your partner also has 4 Spades, so confirms that Spades will be a fit.

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 2S contract. This is showing that they have the Queen as well.
Leading the Queen at trick two also shows that they have it!
You could win your Ace first or second trick, but don't hold it back too long or you might be trumped.
When you have the lead, try to draw out some trumps,
the Ace wins,
and the King,
but someone still has a high Spade. If there is one high trump outstanding, don't draw it.
You should now play your Club winners,
Ace,
King,
Queen,
and Jack, even if you might be trumped.
You should make use
of your remaining little trumps.
At some stage, one of the Defenders will win their Jack of Spades, and you couldn't stop them.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. West passes, since they don't have 12+ points.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. East has less than 12 points, so passes.
You only have 7 points, so you pass.
West also passes.
Your partner opens 1C, showing 12+ points and 3+ Clubs.
You can now come back into the bidding as a Responder with a 1H bid, showing 6+ points, and 4+ Hearts.
Your partner has four Hearts, so confirms the fit with a 2H bid.
There are reasons to go higher, but not this time.

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 2H contract.
They try leading another Diamond,
but you can trump it.
You shold try to draw some trumps with the Ace,
and King, and count them.
There is still one trump against you, and you can't beat it, so leave it alone.
Play some winners in Spades,
and play a third round of Spades,
even though it loses. Your last Spade will be a winner!

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. East has less than 12 points, so passes.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. West has less than 12 ponts, so passes.
Your partner also passes.
East passes too.
You have 12+ points, and so you can open. You should open 1D, you would need 5+ Spades to open 1S.
Your partner Responds 1h, 6+ points and 4+ Hearts.
You offer Spades as a coice, only showing 4 carsd in SApdes the second time.
Partner shows that Spades will be a good fit.

play.teaching: They lead the Two of Clubs against your 2S contract.
They win the King,
and the Ace,
then switch suits to Diamonds.
When you finally get the lead,
try to draw some trumps,
Ace,
Queen,
and King in some order.
Your remaining Diamonds are all winners since the Ace and King were played earlier.

lessons.tip: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. West has less than 12 ponts, so passes.

auction.teaching: Your partner opens 1C, showing 12+ points and 3 or more Clubs.
You can respond 1S with 6 or more points, and 4 or more Spades.

auction.annotation: 25+ combined points, and a Spade fit
auction.teaching: Your partner has enough points to think that your team has a game! They jump to 4S.

play.teaching: They lead the Queen of Diamonds against your 4S contract - showing the Queen and Jack.
You could play the King,
they lead another Diamond,
if you DO play the King
it loses (at trick one or two).
You can trump a Diamond to win the lead.
You should try to draw the trumps,
and again,
and a third time - until the opponents have run out.
You should play your Clubs, and make sure to start with the Ace,
and Queen, "high from the shorter hand".
If you can end in your hand with the Clubs,
you can discard a Heart loser.

lessons.tip: Your partner opens 1C, showing 12+ points and 3 or more Clubs.

auction.teaching: You partner opens 1D, showing 3 or more Diamonds and 12+ points.
You Respond 1H, showing 4+ Hearts, and 6+ points.

auction.annotation: 25+ combined total points with a Heart
auction.teaching: Your partner jumps to game. Partner was adding Shortage points (+5 for a void).

play.teaching: They lead the Queen of Spades against your 4H contract - showing the Jack.
You could play the King, though it will probably lose.
They lead another Spade,
and you still don't play the King.
If they try another Spade,
you can trump them.
You should draw the trumps,
using the Ace,
and King, mopping up all of the trumps.
You should then play Diamonds, starting with the Queen, "high from the shorter hand first",
that way,
you can win the Ace next,
and play all of the Diamonds.

lessons.tip: You partner opens 1D, showing 3 or more Diamonds and 12+ points.

auction.teaching: Click the word DECLARER near the South cards to hide the other three hands. Click NEXT when ready to start. Your partner passes,
so does your opponent,
and you open 1S, showing 5+ Spades and 12+ points.
Your partner raises the Spades, showing a fit (3+ Spades) and 6 - 10 points.
You know that your team has 25+ combined points, so bid to 4S.

play.teaching: They lead the Ten of Clubs against your 4S contract.
You can win the opening lead,
and try to draw the trumps, counting them as you go.
When West is out of Spades, East must still have the Queen.
There is one trump against you, and it is the highest, so leave it alone.
Start playing Heart winners,
and again,
and again,
and again,
even though you will get trumped at some stage.
You can discard a Club loser.
They try a Club,
but you can trump.
You will lose a Diamond at some stage.

auction.annotation: 3+ Spades, close to game, inviting, 11-12 points
auction.teaching: Your partner is close to game, so they jump to 3S to invite you to bid game (11-12 points).
You bid to 4S.

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 4S contract - showing the King and Queen.
You can win the opening lead,
and should try to draw some trumps,
make sure to play your King or Queen on the first trick
to force out the Ace.
You will lose a trick along the way,
but can regain the lead,
and draw the last trump - only losing the Ace, no other trump tricks.
Now you can play your Club winners, make sure to start with the King,
and Jack - "high from the shorter hand".
This will allow you to later win the Ace
and Queen.

and you Respond 1S, showing 4+ Spades and 6+ points.

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 2S contract - top of touching honours.
You can win the lead,
and should try to draw some trumps.
Ace,
and King,
noting that East is out of Spades. There is one trump left (Queen) and you can't beat it, so leave it alone.
You have good Hearts, despite missing the Ace,
so lose the Ace, establishing some Heart tricks.
East knows to lead back a Diamond, from West's opening lead.
Once you regain the lead,
your Hearts are winners.

play.teaching: They lead the King of Diamonds against your 4H contract, top of touching honours.
You can win the lead,
and should try to draw some trumps.
Play the King,
and Ace, capturing all of the opponents trumps, then stop drawing trumps.
You have good Spades, despite missing the Ace.
Lose the Ace, but establish the rest of your Spades.
West wins their Queen, since they forced out your Ace earlier.
When you regain the lead,
play more Spades,
and use the Spades,
to discard low cards.

play.teaching: They lead the Four of Diamonds against your 3NT contract - usually showing an honour, but no sequence.
You can win the lead,
and should start playing Clubs.
After losing the Ace, your remainng Clubs will all be winners.
When you regain the lead,
play more Clubs.
After the Clubs are finished, play your remaining winners in Hearts,
and Spades.

Partner raises you to game in No-Trumps.

play.teaching: They lead the Five of Spades against your 3NT contract - usually showing an honour, but no sequence.
You can win the lead,
and should start playing your longest and best suit, Diamonds.
You must lose the Ace, but the rest of the Diamonds will be winners.
When you regain the lead,
continue playing Diamond winners,
playing the Queen first - "high from the shorter hand".
After the Diamonds,
you can try to establish some Heart tricks as well,
despite losing the Ace.
You can regain the lead in any of the three suits left.
You can then win an additional Heart trick,
as well as your Clubs.

play.teaching: They lead the Jack of Hearts against your 4S contract.
You can win the lead,
and try to draw the trumps,
even though the Ace is missing.
You will lose a trick in Hearts,
but can trump the Heart to win the lead back,

You should play your Clubs (longest side suit), King,
Ace,

auction.teaching: Your partner bids 3S, to offer a choice of games. Partner has five Spades, and wants you to choose which game to play.
With no Spade fit, you return to 3NT.

play.teaching: They lead the Queen of Hearts against your 3NT contract.
You can win the opening Heart lead,
and should start playing Spades right away.
After losing the Ace, the rest of your Spades are winners.
When you regain the lead,
play a Club,
to win in Dummy.
Then play more Spade winners.
After Spades, play the rest of your Clubs,
and Diamonds.

and so do you,

Your partner opens 1C,
and your opponent overcalls 1H.
You can ignore the overcall, and respond 1S.
The opponent raises the Hearts,
and partner bids Spades, all the way to 4S!

play.teaching: They lead the Two of Hearts against your 4S contract.
You can win the Ace,
and play a Spade,
losing the Ace.
You will lose another trick,
but can regain the lead.
You should draw the rest of the trumps,
catching the Queen.
After the opponent's trumps have all been drawn, play your Club winners.

play.teaching: They lead the Jack of Clubs against your 3NT contract.
You can win the lead,
and should play a Diamond which is your longest suit.
You could play the Ace, but you should try the Queen, a FINESSE, hoping that West has the King.
It works!
You should cross back to your hand,
to finesse again,
and if the King is played,
catch it.
After winning all of the Diamonds (or losing the King, but winning the rest), play your Heart winners,
Spade winners,
and Club winners (in any order).

play.teaching: They lead the Jack of Diamonds against your 2H contract.
You can win the lead,
and should draw some trumps,
Ace,
and King,
but the Jack is still out against you.
Stop drawing trumps, and play other winners.

although the Ace is played your King will be established.

and although you lose the Ace your King will be established.
